name: Fake Bank SMS & Email Phishing
summary: A text or email that looks like it came from your bank warns of a suspicious transaction and pushes you to a cloned login page or a phone number staffed by the criminals.

typicalLoss.note: Losses are usually the full drainable balance plus any instant-loan facility the criminal can activate.

howItWorks.detail: You get an SMS, WhatsApp or email: a R4 999 purchase at a store you have never used, a new beneficiary added, or your profile 'locked'. It is engineered to make your stomach drop.
The message gives you exactly one thing to do: click the link to reverse it, or call the number in the message. Both routes lead to the criminals, never to the bank.
The link opens a pixel-accurate copy of your bank's login page on a lookalike domain. Whatever you type is relayed live to a criminal sitting on the real banking site.
The real bank sends you a genuine OTP because a real transaction is being attempted. The fake site or the friendly 'fraud consultant' asks you to read it out or type it in.
Funds move in seconds to a mule account, then to a second and third account, then out as cash or crypto. By the time the bank's fraud desk answers, the trail is cold.

redFlags: The message contains a link. Real banks tell you to use the app you already have.
You are asked to phone a number printed inside the message rather than the one on your card.
Anyone asks you to read out, forward or type an OTP, PIN or full card number.
The domain is nearly right but not right: extra words, hyphens, or an unusual ending.
Extreme time pressure, often a countdown: 'reverse within 10 minutes or the payment clears'.
The greeting is generic ('Dear Client') when your bank normally uses your name.
illustrativeCase: A Durban pensioner receives an SMS at 19:40 saying a R7 300 payment to an electronics retailer is pending. He phones the number in the SMS. A calm, professional 'fraud consultant' confirms the fraud, apologises, and says he will move the money to a secure holding account while the card is cancelled. He reads out three OTPs to authorise the 'reversal'. Each one authorised a real outbound payment. R41 000 gone in under six minutes.
howToProtect: Treat every unexpected bank message as fake until you prove otherwise. Never click, never call the number in the message.
Open the bank's own app, or phone the number physically printed on your bank card, and ask them directly.
Memorise this: no legitimate bank employee will ever ask you for an OTP, PIN or password. There is no exception to this rule.
Set low transaction limits and per-day payment limits in your banking app. It costs you nothing and caps the damage.
Turn on in-app approvals instead of SMS OTPs where your bank offers it.
ifYouveBeenHit: Phone your bank's fraud line immediately, from the number on your card. Speed is the single biggest factor in recovery.
Ask them to freeze the account, reverse or recall the payment, and flag the recipient account.
Change your banking password and PIN from a different, clean device.
Report the incident to the SAPS and get a case number. Your bank will ask for it.
Report the fraudulent number or domain to your bank so it can be taken down for the next person.

faqs.q: The SMS came in the same thread as my real bank messages. Doesn't that prove it is genuine?
faqs.a: No. Sender IDs are trivially spoofed, so a fraudulent message can drop into the same conversation thread as years of genuine ones. Thread position proves nothing at all.

Sometimes, but there is no guarantee. Banks distinguish between unauthorised fraud and transactions you were tricked into authorising yourself. Reporting within minutes materially improves your odds. If you are unhappy with the outcome you can escalate to the National Financial Ombud Scheme.

faqs.q: Is it safer to click the link on a phone or a computer?
faqs.a: Neither is safe. Phishing pages capture credentials identically on both, and phone screens hide the full URL, which makes them slightly worse.
